Environmental Health & Safety Incident Log - Building 7, Chem Lab Wing
Submitted by: Lab Manager Oluwaseun Bello
Date of incident: May 22, 2026

I want to document this thoroughly since we had a few things happen around the same time and I want the record to be clear about what was and wasn't related to the actual spill. Tuesday started normally, we had a scheduled delivery of new glassware in the morning which took longer than expected to unpack and inventory, probably ate up two hours of Priya's and my time before lunch, but that's not really incident-relevant, just context for why the lab was a bit more cluttered than usual with boxes near the east bench.

Around 1:40pm, grad student Felix Adeyemi was transferring approximately 400mL of acetone from a bulk container into smaller working bottles at the fume hood on the east bench when the glass bulk container, which we later determined had a hairline crack we didn't know about, gave way and roughly 250mL spilled onto the hood surface and a small amount, maybe 20-30mL, dripped onto the floor beneath the hood. The fume hood sash was down at the appropriate working height and the hood was operating normally, so fumes were contained reasonably well; our air monitoring badge in that bay didn't show any reading above baseline afterward. Felix was wearing the required PPE (goggles, gloves, lab coat) and none of the acetone contacted his skin or eyes - he stepped back immediately and was not injured in any way, though he did say it startled him given the sound of the glass cracking.

We evacuated just that bay of the lab, not the whole building or even the whole room, while Priya and I did the cleanup per the acetone SDS spill procedure: absorbent pads, proper disposal into the flammables waste container, ventilation continued running. Total cleanup took about 25 minutes. No fire occurred, acetone is flammable but there was no ignition source active in that bay at the time since the bench burner in that bay had been shut off for the glassware delivery anyway, which in hindsight was a lucky coincidence, not a safety measure we can take credit for.

Separately and I want to be very clear this is UNRELATED to the spill: later that same afternoon, around 4pm, a different student, Marcus, in the biology wing two floors up, reported feeling dizzy and was sent to student health, but that building has independent ventilation from ours and the timing was coincidental, biology has confirmed it was unrelated to any chemical exposure, they think he just skipped lunch and it was low blood sugar. I only mention it because a rumor started circulating that 'someone was overcome by fumes' and I want the record to clearly separate that unrelated, resolved-as-non-incident from our actual acetone spill, since I've already had two people ask me about it thinking they were the same event.

The cracked bulk container has been sent to our glassware vendor for inspection since this is the second cracked container from that same lot number in three months (the first crack, in March, didn't result in a spill since it was noticed before use). We're pausing use of that lot number pending vendor response. No injuries resulted from today's spill, no fire, no evacuation beyond the immediate bay, and air monitoring showed no elevated readings. Recommending the incident be classified as a minor spill, no injury, contained, for our monthly EHS report.

One more administrative note for whoever files this: Priya is going to update the east bench inventory sheet tomorrow since a few of the smaller working bottles we were transferring into got knocked around during the cleanup and we want to double check none of them cracked too, though a quick visual check today didn't show any damage to those. We're also going to ask the glassware vendor whether the whole shipment from that delivery this morning should be inspected before use, out of an abundance of caution, even though only the one bulk container from a much older order was actually involved in today's spill. I'll follow up with an addendum once the vendor responds and once we hear back about whether Marcus in biology is feeling better, purely so we can close the loop on the rumor and confirm in writing, for anyone reading this later, that the two events were unrelated.

Incident IR-PRIV-119

A customer emailed asking why they received a promotional email addressed to a different customer's name in the subject line, though the email body and offer were correct for them. We investigated: this was traced to a template rendering bug in our email tool that occasionally pulled the wrong 'first name' merge field when two customers' records were processed in the same batch within 50 milliseconds of each other, a timing race condition. It affected an estimated 340 emails out of a 1.2 million email campaign send (about 0.028%). No other personal data (address, payment info, order history) was included or exposed - only a first name field was swapped, and only within the subject line greeting. Initial theory was a database export error exposing full customer records to the wrong recipients, but engineering confirmed this was ruled out: no email contained another customer's full record, order details, or contact information, only a misapplied first name. We are notifying the 340 affected customers per policy, though this does not meet the legal threshold for a reportable data breach in our jurisdiction since no sensitive personal data was exposed.

Postmortem Draft - Incident INC-5502, Payments API Degradation

Timeline (all times UTC): 09:12 - Alerting fired for elevated 5xx error rate on the payments-api service (spiked from baseline ~0.1% to 14.8%). 09:15 - On-call engineer Kwame Asante acknowledged the page. 09:22 - Kwame posted in the incident Slack channel: 'Looks like the database connection pool is exhausted, investigating why.' 09:40 - Root cause identified: a deploy at 08:55 had reduced the connection pool size config from 100 to 10 due to a copy-paste error in the config file, not an actual infrastructure failure. 09:44 - Fix deployed (pool size restored to 100). 09:51 - Error rate back to baseline (0.09%).

Total duration of elevated errors: 09:12 to 09:51 = 39 minutes. Our SLA commits to 99.9% monthly uptime, which allows for about 43 minutes of downtime per 30-day month; however, this incident was degraded performance (14.8% error rate), not full downtime, so per our SLA definitions (which only count full outages, not partial degradation, toward the uptime figure) this incident does NOT count against the monthly uptime SLA number, though it is still logged as a customer-impacting incident for internal tracking.

Separately, in the same Slack thread, a different engineer, Fatima Rahman, mentioned she was 'also seeing weird latency on the notifications-service around the same time' but after investigation this was determined to be unrelated - notifications-service had a pre-scheduled maintenance window at that exact time that explains its latency fully, confirmed by the maintenance calendar. Fatima's comment is included here only because it caused some initial confusion during triage about whether this was a wider outage.

Approximately 2,400 payment transactions were affected (retried automatically by client SDKs in 94% of cases with no customer-visible failure; the remaining 6%, about 144 transactions, surfaced a visible error to the end customer and would need manual customer support follow-up). Action items: (1) add a config-diff review step to the deploy pipeline requiring a second approver for any connection-pool or resource-limit changes, owner Kwame, due in 2 weeks; (2) add an automated alert specifically for connection pool utilization crossing 80%, owner platform team, due in 3 weeks.
